Whereas all Canadians are aware of the situation in Poland, and whereas all Canadians are aware of the plight of the Polish refugees in the camps in Austria, and whereas Canada has always come to the aid of those in need, notwithstanding established immigration quotas, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Don Valley West (Mr. Bosley):

subsubtopic: NEED FOR WORKING CAPITAL-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on an urgent matter brought to our attention via the eighth International Symposium on Small Business. Canada's extremely high interest rates have made it virtually impossible for a growing number of small businesses to maintain sufficient flows of operating capital, yet present federal financial programs provide virtually no assistance in this area. The survival of Canada's small business sector is being threatened by the present shortage of working capital. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans):
That the government open up the Small Businesses Loans Act and the small business development bond to allow entrepreneurs access to working capital and thereby stop the demise of our vital small business community.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Since the government took office in 1980 it has given us high interest rates, loss of our homes, a 43-cent dollar, an unnecessary postal strike, regional tensions destroying national unity, a shattered rail system, and government by closure and order in council. It is destroying Parliament. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers):
That, due to the Prime Minister's lack of leadership and total lack of compassion and understanding of important issues, this House asks him to allow democracy to take its course and instructs him to resign his administration and
to call an election, thus allowing Canadians to replace his uncaring government with a government ready to respond to the challenge facing this nation.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to move a motion under Standing Order 43. The government is ignoring old age pensioners. One of my constituents writes:
I don't get to visit and used to enjoy Christmas and birthday cards. Now they are cut to a minimum. I gave up smoking. I do my own hair and make clothes last, and am still fighting a losing battle. I went through the depression and worry that history is repeating itself.
I move, therefore, seconded by the hon. member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson):
That this House urge the Minister of Finance to cease flogging the dead horse of the $35 increase in the Guaranteed Income Supplement, and do something meaningful to alleviate the plight of people, such as my constituent, by repudiating his high interest rate policy, thereby ceasing to practise monetary policy at the expense of the poor and aged.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of some urgency. The former postmaster general announced that, at the beginning of the new year, the cost to consumers of stamps and postal services will rise significantly, the basic letter rate increasing to 30 cents. In light of the fact that postal rate increases and costly modernization have never noticeably improved basic service, and the fact that the proposed new increases will be of considerable hardship to thousands of Canadians, particularly senior citizens who rely on the daily mail for everyday business and personal use, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastines (Mr. Ellis):
That the government be soundly condemned for planning such an excessive increase in postal rates as a means of improving the postal service and structure, and that the postmaster general take immediate steps to ensure the increase is reduced to a more modest and appropriate level.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN INTEREST RATES
speechtext: We have made a suggestion to the Minister of Agriculture about how to provide financing for the agricultural community at reasonable interest rates. In the latter part of August the Minister of Agriculture made a commitment that he would provide money to farmers at 14 per cent through the Farm Credit Corporation. Did the Minister of Agriculture take our suggestion to cabinet? If farmers are to receive the benefit of money at 14 per cent through the Farm Credit Corporation, why, within four weeks of his promise, did he allow Farm Credit interest rates to go from 14 per cent to nearly 17 per cent?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN INTEREST RATES
speechtext: I do not know what the hon. member is referring to, Madam Speaker. Any minister in charge of interest rate programs would like to see the interest rate as low as possible. The Farm Credit Corporation uses the past six months average cost of money for their formula. This worked out to 16% per cent. It was automatically triggered. We had discussions about freezing it at 14 per cent. I do not remember-and I will check all the tapes again-in my many speeches where I mentioned 14 per cent. I believe the furthest I would have gone was to say I would do my utmost to see it stayed at 14 per cent. However, I have no recollection of making a firm commitment that it would stay at 14 per cent.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
To help the minister's memory, the commitment was made in an interview after he spoke to the Canadian National Exhibition last August.
The minister has further stated publicly he will either get money for farmers at 14 per cent or he will resign. Could the minister give us the time frame in which we can expect one or the other? Or does he intend to cop out?

I am not so sure that a general infusion of funds into the Farm Credit Corporation is the answer to the special difficulties of certain groups of farmers in the country.

(CANCOM) would be allowed to distribute a package of Canadian radio and television signals to northern communities across the country. Subsequently many smaller northern and remote communities through their municipal councils applied to the CRTC to be terrestrial distributors. Now, however, the CRTC has ruled that municipal corporations may not be issued broadcasting licences because of chapter 377 of the Broadcasting Act which is an order directing the CRTC that municipal corporations are ineligible. Subsequent to that the CRTC wrote to these municipalities-

speechtext: Thank you, Madam Speaker. subsubtopic: IMPORTATION OF JAPANESE CARS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. On June 4, 1981, the minister announced quite proudly that Japanese automakers had agreed to reduce voluntarily the number of their exports to Canada by 6 per cent. At that time the minister said that the growing number of automotive imports into Canada was contributing considerably toward the high unemployment level. In an answer to a question in the House at the same time the minister assured us that there would be a substantial increase in the Canadian content of offshore imports. Being the accommodating fellow I am, I should like to give the minister an opportunity to report on the progress he has made since then, with regard to both the voluntary Japanese restraint program and the additional Canadian content in offshore imports, as promised by the minister.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: IMPORTATION OF JAPANESE CARS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the arrangements the Japanese announced on June 4 cover the fiscal year from April 1, 1981, to April 1, 1982. They said they would restrain their exports to Canada in that period to some 174,000 units. At the time the
Oral Questions
arrangements were announced, exports for the period after April 1 to June were already under way, which was reflected in some increase in exports. I am happy to report that in August of this year there was a sharp drop in exports from Japan to some 11,000 units from the 19,000 level in the previous month. I look forward to this level being maintained for the balance of the fiscal year. If that is the case, the level the Japanese said they would maintain certainly would be achieved.
With respect to the achievement of greater Canadian content in imports, I want to confirm to the House that we have had a major achievement because of the agreement of the federal government to enter into a special duty remission program with Volkswagen Canada. They said that they would be establishing a plant which will hire some 500 people. They will be doubling the purchase of parts from independent Canadian manufacturers to some $150 million per year, with some 1,500 jobs. They will be maintaining a Canadian content level after 1983 of some 84 per cent, much higher than is the case required for existing Canadian manufacturers. I thank my friend for his constructive question.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I cannot believe the minister tried to answer that question with a straight face. He knows full well that since April 1 the number of Japanese automotive imports has increased to 90,893 vehicles, an increase of over 70 per cent. Even though that increase dropped somewhat in August, if this trend continues for one or two months they will never keep that promise. It is like the minister's industrial strategy. It has evaporated. His promise on the automotive industry has not materialized, and he is still here despite the high interest rates which are plaguing the country.
My supplementary question is directed to the same minister. Is he now prepared to be honest with Canadians, admit his failures in the auto industry, and at the same time revise his expectations regarding Japanese imports as well as Canadian content in Japanese automobiles and vehicles, as the minister promised, so that the industry can plan accordingly? Can the minister give us that undertaking now?

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, certainly I do not accept the premise of the hon. member's question. We made efforts which were reflected in our arrangements with Chrysler, Ford, and other companies, as well as independent parts manufacturers that are moving toward the achievement of the objective of a stronger Canadian industry. Also we have begun to move toward our objective of greater Canadian content with respect to exports to Canada of companies not established here. The hon. member's premise is quite wrong. There is a lot more room and ground to cover. We are working actively to pursue and fulfil those objectives. I do not think my hon. friend is on the right track at all. In fact, from his questions he is right off

Oral Questions
the road when it comes to knowing what he is talking about with regard to automobiles.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance in view of the significance of his budget for Canadians, of which the minister is well aware. The minister has already told me that he would be able to table his budget before the end of October and he finally announced officially November 3 as the date of the budget. Can the minister tell the House today whether it would have been physically possible for him to table his budget before November 3 if it had not been for this conference?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Keeping in mind the great many lay-offs in the footwear industry, particularly so in Quebec, and the ever growing share of the market cornered by imports, that is, already 58 per cent of the Canadian market, and this percentage having followed an upward trend especially since the devaluation of foreign currencies, can the minister tell the House whether he intends to maintain the import quotas as recommended in the report of the Anti-dumping Tribunal respecting the footwear industry?

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER FOOTWEAR IMPORTATION QUOTAS RECOMMENDED BY ANTI-DUMPING TRIBUNAL WILL BE MAINTAINED

Madam Speaker, my colleague has accurately described the problem of the footwear industry. We in cabinet take this problem very seriously. That is why we are very actively discussing our policy for that industry. We are fully aware of the fact that our current quota system will end December 1, and I want to assure my colleague and the House that within the next few weeks we will be in a position to clarify our policy. I hope it will be possible to set the footwear industry and its labour force well at ease.

subsubtopic: EXERCISE OF SPECIAL POWERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Solicitor General, the minister responsible for ensuring that the RCMP obey the law in Canada. The Solicitor General has said that in his view the rule of law justifies a number of illegal activities which the McDonald Commission strongly urged be validated by legislation. He further indicated that he is continuing to authorize the RCMP to engage in activities which McDonald stated clearly violate the law.
In view of the fact that the McDonald Commission stated that tolerating any breaches of the law is merely the thin edge of the wedge, how can the Solicitor General defend his dangerous statements allowing the RCMP to decide which laws it is reasonably necessary to break, statements which clearly say that there is one law for the RCMP and another law for all other Canadians?

subsubtopic: EXERCISE OF SPECIAL POWERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: EXERCISE OF SPECIAL POWERS
speechtext:
I could certainly never justify that policy in the manner the hon. member opposite has attributed to me. What I did say, and in which I am supported by the law officers of the Crown and by some outside law opinions, is that there are special powers which are available to the police which are not available to ordinary citizens in the course of law enforcement activities, when it is reasonably necessary for them to exercise those powers. I think Canadians are very pleased and satisfied with the level of effective law enforcement that we have in this country, and I do not propose to see that diminished.

October 21, 1981
Oral Questions

subsubtopic: EXERCISE OF SPECIAL POWERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: EXERCISE OF SPECIAL POWERS
speechtext: The RCMP is complying, in its activities, with the rule of law. Therefore, to characterize its activities as illegal is totally unjustified. In fact McDonald himself did not say that they were unlawful; he said that they were not authorized by law, which is not the same thing as saying that they are unlawful.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: Madam Speaker, with that kind of contemptuous attitude the minister himself should be charged with aiding and abetting violations of the Criminal Code.
Oh, oh!

My supplementary question to that co-conspirator is this: as a result of yesterday's Supreme Court of Canada's decision allowing the RCMP to breach the privacy of Canadians' confidential medical records, will the Solicitor General assure this House that under no circumstances will he allow the RCMP to request such confidential medical information from health care personnel in violation of laws, regulations, and possibly medical ethics?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I gather that my friend opposite is now calling the decisions of the Supreme Court of Canada unlawful.
I directed that appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada when we had the decision of the court of appeal because I felt it was necessary for the RCMP and all of the other police forces in Canada as well to have a privilege in their relationship with informers. The Supreme Court of Canada has upheld that privilege. To suggest those activities are unlawful after the Supreme Court of Canada itself found that they were lawful is, to my way of thinking, a very grave and political distortion of what happened at the Supreme Court of Canada.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Numerous representations were made last winter, and again this spring and summer, concerning health hazards in certain Cree villages at James Bay. I should like to know whether the minister has done anything to improve sanitary conditions on the James Bay coast?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Begin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: MEASURES TO IMPROVE SANITARY CONDITIONS AMONG JAMES BAY CREE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to say to the hon.
member that, through its parliamentary committee, the House has been made aware that all summer long we did closely monitor the question of the health of the James Bay Cree Indians, in co-operation with the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and following a joint meeting of our officials and the ministers involved, as well as the health conditions in each of the villages whose environmental conditions were critical, so as to ensure that the various parties involved were discharging their responsibilities. Before making my submissions to you, which are submissions in an area quite different from those made by the hon. member for Oshawa, may I point out that in Hansard at page 11912 for October 19, the issue now before the Chair is listed under the heading "Privilege". There is no mention made of a point of order. Similarly, in the index there is no mention made of a point of order. That oversight is carried forward into yesterday's Hansard.
I suggest for future reference, when one wishes to have access to these jewels of wisdom coming from hon. members and from the Chair, that in order to made it easier, it might be well to suggest to the Hansard office that they do list a point of order raised as such. There were the two questions, as the Chair will recall. There was a distinct question of privilege and a distinct question of order. It is to the latter that I wish to speak today.
October 21, 1981

The key citation mentioned by the hon. member for Oshawa comes from Beauchesne's fifth edition, Citation 327(2), which reads:
It has been admitted that a document which has been cited ought to be laid upon the Table of the House, if it can be done without injury to the public interest.
The hon. member for Oshawa rested his submission and argument on the interpretation of the word "cited" as meaning "quoted", or a document quoted from. I wish to carry the submission beyond that and refer the Chair to the same Citation 327, but to paragraph (5), where in effect Beauchesne sets forth the definition of the word "cite". It reads:
To be cited, a document must be quoted or specifically used to influence debate.
In my submission, citing a document means two different things. Either the document must be quoted from or it must be specifically used to influence debate. The admission that a document exists or the reading of the salutation or address of a letter does not constitute a citing.
My submissions to you, Madam Speaker, will be resting on the argument that the document itself has been used extensively for three days in a row now to support a certain position taken by the minister in debate and, on the other hand, to support a certain position taken by the hon. member for Oshawa.
This cannot be gainsaid. If one refers to page 11906 of Hansard, it will be seen that the minister did attempt "to influence debate", to use the words of Beauchesne. He did this by specifically using the document in an attempt to influence his side of the question, not only with the hon. member for Oshawa but with the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and others on this side of the House. That appears in the right-hand column of Hansard for October 19, 1981, at page 11906 and again at 11907, where the minister went so far as to use certain figures in the document and deny the validity of other figures. The minister carried on with that yesterday in his attempt to influence the debate as to the validity or invalidity of the document.
At page 11970 of Hansard for October 20, the minister responded to a submission I made to the Chair. In part, the minister said:
I would say further that there is nothing in the report that was not in the newspapers yesterday.
He had other references in the edition of Hansard for October 20 which clearly can bring one to no other conclusion but that the minister was using the document to influence the position he was taking in the debate on the subject matter of the document, namely housing.
The key points under debate at the time were, may it please the Chair, first, that the minister referred twice to figures in the document; that was up to today. Today the minister made further reference to those figures. In addition, he referred to the cut-off in disposable income earmarked for housing. Very clearly those references are recorded in Hansard.
Point of Order-Mr. Broadbent
The second point I wish to submit to you, Madam Speaker, is that the House is placed in a position where there is a dispute between four members now, namely, the minister, the hon. member for Oshawa, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). My submission to you is that the rest of the members of this place are placed in the position that they cannot participate in debate because the document is not before them. Certainly it is not before any members on this side, although the minister's generosity has apparently extended to at least one and probably more members on his own side of the House.
I would just draw your attention, Madam Speaker, to the fact that this situation places all other members in the position that we cannot participate in this debate to determine which side of the argument we may wish to come down on. We are prevented from doing it because the document is not before us. It is my submission that this is precisely the situation that the rule respecting the tabling of cited documents was intended to avoid. In saying "cited" I take the definition in paragraph (5) of Citation 327, namely, that the document was "specifically used to influence debate".
The minister has attacked the document to support his view of the housing crisis. The Leader of the Opposition and others on this side have put forward the document as supporting the point of view exactly to the contrary. Members cannot appreciate whether the minister's reflections are accurate unless they see the document and understand the context in which the figures were used and how much the argument was dependent upon them.
In summary, therefore, I submit to you there can be no doubt that the document exists. From the minister's own mouth it was prepared in his own department, he has read it now, and since having read it he has again used it to influence debate. If it is in the possession of the minister and some other members opposite, it is the focus of debate and the minister has cited parts of it in a bad light to make his own case to influence debate. Members cannot evaluate the document or intelligently participate in discussion of it unless it is tabled so as to give all members a look at it. That is the purpose of the rule, in my submission. The minister has used the document to influence debate. Therefore, that constitutes a citing of the document and I ask the Chair to find accordingly and require the tabling by the minister of the document which has been used these past three days.

speakeroldname: Hon. Yvon Pinard (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. BROADBENT-OBLIGATION OF MINISTER TO TABLE DOCUMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, after listening to my hon. colleague, I have the impression I have heard the same thing many times before in this House, and in fact it is not the first time the opposition party has invoked Citation 327(5) to claim that even if a minister had not purposely quoted part of a document, he had used it to influence debate.

October 21, 1981
Point of Order-Mr. Broadbent
I may point out, Madam Speaker, that the entire line of reasoning used by the member for Yukon is based on replies given by the minister in question on October 19, 1981, on pages 11906 and following of Hansard, that is, during question period.
I should like to start by saying that question period has never been considered as a debate and does not constitute a debate, and consequently, it is impossible to claim during question period that a minister is trying to influence debate, because there is no debate. So, if there is no debate, my hon. colleague's line of reasoning cannot stand. The fact that reference was made to a document cannot, during the oral question period, constitute an attempt to influence debate, since we are not involved in a debate. In fact, according to parliamentary practice and rules, there is no debate during the oral question period.
We must also consider the context of the replies given, and we have here a subsidiary argument put forward by the minister. Allow me to read part of the first question which was asked by the leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent). Madam Speaker, what we should remember is that the document in question was invoked at the very beginning by a member of the opposition, by the Leader of the New Democratic Party, who said in his question on page 11906, and I quote:
Another report did emerge on the weekend from CMHC, this one contending that 135 families a day-
The Toronto Star has a copy of the report, and I have a copy of the report, and then the leader of the New Democratic Party asked his question. So the document in question was first used by a member of the opposition. It would be grossly unfair to prevent a minister from referring in his reply to the question that was directed to him. With due respect, the minister in question had absolutely no choice but to refer to the documents invoked by a member of the opposition. But referring does not constitute quoting, and because the document was invoked by a member of the opposition, the document was not referred to in an attempt to influence debate, because debate had not been sought by the minister. The document was invoked by a member of the opposition and, I repeat, the oral question period does not constitute a debate. Finally, Madam Speaker, parliamentary practice and the authorities are quite definite about this, Beauchesne's Citation 327(3) on page 116 is quite clear in this respect, and I feel this should be the basis for any decision in this type of argument, and I quote:
A public document referred to but not cited or quoted by a minister need not be tabled.
This is a general principle which certainly applies here. Further on in Citation 327(4), the same principle prevails:
Only the document cited need be tabled by a minister.
Here again, unless a quote has been taken from the document, there can be no obligation to table the document. And finally, section (5), and I quote:
To be cited, a document must be quoted-
-which is not the case-
-or specifically used to influence debate.
For reasons I have already mentioned, and I do not intend to go over them again, there was no attempt during the oral question period to influence debate on a document invoked by a member of the opposition.
Therefore, Madam Speaker, I submit that the point raised by the member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) has no basis at all, it has no basis in fact. We have a general principle that a minister is not obliged to table a document he has not quoted, and a minister cannot influence debate during the oral question period, because the oral question period is not a debate.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. BROADBENT-OBLIGATION OF MINISTER TO TABLE DOCUMENT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member has raised an additional point I did not touch on. In two sentences I will submit to you that whether or not the question period constitutes a debate has been decided by your predecessor and, I believe, by yourself as well. The decision is that it does, indeed, constitute a debate for the purpose of this citation.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subtopic: MR. BROADBENT-OBLIGATION OF MINISTER TO TABLE DOCUMENT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would join briefly in the discussion you have before you. The question you have before you as to whether or not the minister in any way made reference directly to the document I think is quite clear.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. BROADBENT-OBLIGATION OF MINISTER TO TABLE DOCUMENT
speechtext: He does not have to.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subtopic: MR. BROADBENT-OBLIGATION OF MINISTER TO TABLE DOCUMENT
speechtext:
I am not suggesting he has to. I am suggesting, however, he did. Citation 327 of Beauchesne reads:
A Minister of the Crown is not at liberty to read or quote from a despatch or other state paper not before the House, unless he is prepared to lay it upon the Table.
I put to you that, as recorded at page 11906 of Hansard for October 19, 1981, in answer to a question from my leader, the minister said:
1 would ask the Clerk to return the report to him so thay he may reread the paper. I have, on two seconds reading, identified that they are talking about interest rates of 22 per cent.
The minister corrected, in his estimation, my leader's submission, pointing out that the document referred to a figure of 22 per cent.
I submit to you, Madam Speaker, that clearly was an effort by the minister to influence the course of the debate by quoting directly from a page in the document. On those grounds alone, without entering into any further argument, I suggest you could find only that the minister did in fact quote from the document.
October 21, 1981

I suppose the question before Your Honour now is, should the document be tabled. I submit that Beauchesne is clear, that where it has been reasonably decided that the minister did in fact quote from, or make direct reference to, a public document for the purpose of influencing a debate or, for that matter, influencing opinion in the House of Commons, the practice of tabling the document has generally been acquiesced. Rather than carry this on at great length, I would simply ask that the minister do what Beauchesne indicates most people in these circumstances have done in the past, and that is simply table the document.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. BROADBENT-OBLIGATION OF MINISTER TO TABLE DOCUMENT
speechtext:
The resolution of this question would flow out of the definition one would give to what "citing" or "quoting". I suggest that a common sense definition of that would be that the minister would have to read quite extensively from a document in order to call it a quote. If he is referring to a figure that is in a document, or to a sentence or word, especially when it is in answer to a question put to him by another member of the House and that document is subsequently sent over to the minister so he may glance at whatever is referred to, I would say it is very difficult for me to find that the minister was, at that time, quoting from the document.
The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), in quoting from Beauchesne, tried to pin his argument on the fact that Beauchesne does say that the document must be quoted in order to be tabled or specifically used to influence the debate.
I will not enter into the question whether question period is debate or not. Some Speakers have determined that sometimes it is debate. My interpretation is that it is not debate. I suggest that Beauchesne was not using the word "debate" in this particular sense when writing this paragraph.
I would also suggest that to be clear on what that paragraph means it should read that the document must be quoted "and" specifically used, rather than "or" specifically used to influence debate. The word "or" is a bit ambiguous. It means you could either quote from it or use it to further an argument, which I think did not happen in this particular case.
In support of my ruling, I would also refer hon. members to what actually happened. The hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) has quoted the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove), when he returned the document to the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), as having said that the member for Oshawa "may reread the paper". He did not say he had read it; he said the member for Oshawa may reread it, and I think we know that it was not read in the House.
The hon. member for Oshawa may have read it in his office but it was not quoted in the House. Then the member for Oshawa replied that the minister had not taken the trouble to read the document before returning it to him. So that was an admission made by the hon. member for Oshawa and it does support my position that nobody has quoted from or cited that document.
In this case the question which has to be resolved is whether the minister should be obligated to table that document. Since

the rule applies to an obligation to table the document if a member has quoted from it, I must find that the minister may table the document if he so wishes; but I am in no position, according to our rules, to force him to do so.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on a point of order, I am not questioning any ruling which you have made but I fear we may be getting on to an undesirable track. With great respect, it may be the advice you are receiving, but there is nothing that I can find in the applicable Standing Order that requires unanimous consent. In my submission, paragraph (8) of that Standing Order gives the Chair a discretion.
Further, that discretion is placed in the hands of the Chair in order to protect the rights of members. With great respect, asking for unanimous consent is not an adequate protection of those rights because it is delegating that responsibility to government members who are going to say "no" to everything. If we get into taking this direction as a permanent part of our procedure, no petition will ever be discussed, even if in your discretion you might believe it necessary, because you will have established the precedent of requiring unanimous consent.
I submit that that question should be looked at very carefully. If the Chair chooses to exercise its discretion in the negative, that is fine, that has to be accepted; but I respectfully submit that asking for unanimous consent is not the correct way to proceed.

However, prior to asking for unanimous consent I did tell the hon. member that if I were to use my discretion, I would feel that the matter is not urgent and does not require immediate debate.
I believe the petition calls for a change in the Standing Orders. The Standing Orders have existed for a long time. We
have been ruled by them for a number of years. Therefore, if the hon. member would like to see some changes in the Standing Orders he is, of course, allowed to discuss and to ask for that. subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I too would like to speak to the motion put forth by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger) since it deals directly with an issue which is of critical importance to northerners, particularly my constituents.
I first wish to quote from an article by Douglas Fisher which appeared in The Toronto Sun on Monday, May 11, 1981 in which he quoted former United States President James Monroe:
The hunter or savage state requires a greater extent of territory to sustain it than is compatible with the progress and just claims of civilized life ... and must yield to it.
Might I suggest that Bill C-48 can be called the "Canadian Monroe". This was written in 1817. Therefore, I believe that Bill C-48 is an anachronism that is appropriate to the government across the way. In a general sense, this motion by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin tries to ensure that Bill C-48 will not prejudice the outcome of land claims negotiations which are currently going on between the Government of Canada and various native organizations across the north. The minister has repeatedly assured members of the standing committee of this House that Bill C-48 is neutral with regard to land claims in the north. He also said that passage of this bill will have no effect whatsoever on the outcome of these delicate negotiations.
However much I would like to, I am unable to accept that view and would like to give an explanation as to why. For the minister to say to us that land claims negotiations will not be jeopardized or affected by this bill indicates only too clearly that he lacks a precise understanding of what land claims are

October 21, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
all about. It is about time his understanding was improved, and I will be only too happy to assist.
First, let me talk about what land claims are not. Land claims are not a process whereby the aboriginal peoples of Canada give up all rights to their lands, especially those in the north, in exchange for some simple form of compensation which Bill C-48 does not even propose. This once-and-for-all type of approach worked for the government in the nineteenth century and, however much it would like to continue the practice today, the government must recognize the fact that it is no longer acceptable to the northern peoples.
There is a famous saying which says: "Those who do not learn from their mistakes are destined to repeat them". The people of the north are only too aware of the consequences of selling off their rights in the way that the government would prefer. They see how others in the south have been robbed of their own economic resource base, confined to reserves and left marginalized within their own home lands by accepting the government's approach to the making of treaties and the settling of claims.
The government is now inviting the native people to sit down and agree to the same types of settlements, in effect, to repeat the mistakes of the past; but all northern peoples say "no". They have a different vision of what land claims are all about. To them, comprehensive claims are the means by which their rights to the land and its resources will be recognized and entrenched. They are not approaching the government with the position that "everything must remain ours". On the contrary, they recognize that the resources that exist in their home lands are needed by their fellow Canadians and they are willing to share them.
But they do see land claims settlements as the vehicle which will ensure that the mistakes of the past will not be repeated. They seek to define, very clearly, their relationship with the larger society before development activities disrupt their communities irreparably-I emphasize that-and it is through land claims negotiations that they seek to accomplish this. They want to define, for instance, who owns the land, including surface and subsurface rights, and also how decisions will be made in the future regarding land use management, environmental protection and a variety of other crucial matters. In short, they want to define their economic and political rights for the future in such a way as to ensure that their needs continue to be met at least as much as those of southerners. They are not willing to become marginalized in their home lands, either economically or politically. They have made it very clear to the government that they are not simply out for a "quick buck", but want to reach settlements which will guarantee them a continual say over matters which so obviously affect them.
Over the last few years, organizations representing the peoples of the north have met with the government to discuss these matters on the assumption that they could be resolved through a process of negotiation. In fact, it was the government in its 1973 policy statement on native claims in Canada which recommended this process as the best way to achieve solutions. The native peoples have responded to this invitation in good faith and have produced, in a relatively short time, fairly sophisticated proposals which they feel would protect their interests and allow them to maintain their viability within the context of Canadian federalism.
I should like to note that in the next few months there will be a plebiscite in the Northwest Territories to determine the political evolution of the north, but this is opposed.
At the same time as it is pretending to negotiate a solution to these fundamental questions in the context of land claims, however, the government has brought forth Bill C-48. Bill C-48 stipulates that all revenues from oil and gas developments north of 60 are to go directly to the federal government, with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) having a remarkable degree of discretion to decide on the nature, pace and location of all resource developments in the area, something no other minister has ever had. Through Bill C-48 the federal government is serving notice to everyone involved that it sees these northern resources as its property to control and benefit from as it sees fit.
Coming as it does, when the government is also negotiating the ownership of northern lands and resources with the northern peoples, the bill forces us to conclude that the government is speaking out of both sides of its mouth. If we liken the present situation to that of the ownership of a house which is in dispute, we can perhaps see more clearly the injustice of the government's actions and the extent to which they will affect the outcome of claims negotiations by the Dene, COPE, the ITC and others in the north. Take, for example, a house, the ownership of which is in dispute. Two parties say they have a claim to the ownership of the house and its contents, some of which are extremely valuable. Each side acknowledges that the other has a claim, and instead of going through the courts to find a solution, the two sides agree that the whole matter can best be resolved through a process of negotiation.
While these agreed-upon negotiations are taking place, however, one party suddenly announces that it is taking over all the valuable contents of the house with the intention of selling them. Legally, this party's right to dispose of property on which there is an outstanding claim by a third party would appear dubious. And morally, such actions would be reprehensible at best, and would call into serious question the party's stated desire to achieve a negotiated settlement.
This is what the federal government is doing with Bill C-48. It is giving the northern peoples two different messages: one, it is saying: "We accept the fact that you have a legitimate claim to the areas of the north in question"; and second, it is also declaring that the resources on those lands and the right to decide how and when they will be developed belong solely to the federal government. By bringing forth Bill C-48 at this time, the government has, therefore, succeeded in making a mockery of the negotiation process which it initiated in 1973 through one of its own policies.
October 21, 1981

The government responds to these types of charges by saying that it needs to consolidate its powers over oil and gas development in the north in order to manage them more effectively for the interests of northerners; that it needs to control the revenue from developments for the national interest, but that sufficient funds would always be returned to the north to ensure that residents there receive benefits. In other words, welfare. By this, the government is simply saying: "We will control everything relating to development in the north, but don't you northerners worry, we will continue to look after you". It is time that northerners, Mr. Speaker, native and non-native alike-and I represent them all-were allowed to look after themselves. It is time they were free of the kind of paternalism that Bill C-48 represents: It is time that they be allowed to have a say in the decisions which will affect them clearly. Bill C-48 succeeds in denying them all of these.
In response to the charge that Bill C-48 will undermine or prejudice the outcome of current land claims negotiations, the minister says that nothing could be further from the truth. He has stated time and time again, and with great assurance, that the provisions of the bill will not affect the substance of an eventual settlement in any way. He assures us that changes can always be made to this legislation in the future in order to accommodate the terms of any settlements. In other words, he is saying that, in spite of the terms of the current bill, everything still remains negotiable in the context of future claims negotiations, including presumably the question of the ownership of surface and subsurface resources. "Trust us", he has said to us many times. He is saying to the native peoples: "We will be willing to negotiate anything you want in the future, despite what Bill C-48 says."
While they would no doubt like to trust in the government's good intentions on this issue, the northern peoples are understandably reluctant to do so and for good reasons. They stem from the fact that, in the context of negotiations that have occurred to date, the federal government has been decidedly unwilling to negotiate the question of ownership of subsurface resources. In the only agreement that has been reached to date, that signed between the government and the Committee for Original People's Entitlement in the fall of 1978, it was clearly stipulated that northern peoples would not be allowed to select lands on which there were known oil or gas deposits. When the agreement was announced, the then minister of Indian affairs and northern development was quick to announce to other native groups that they could not expect a better deal than that which was struck with COPE.
Therefore, throughout the history of the negotiations the government has placed very strong limits on what it considers to be negotiable. It has said that the ownership of subsurface mineral rights is non-negotiable to all intents and purposes, and on the matters relating to political rights, these too have been effectively excluded from the process of negotiation. Despite the desire of northern peoples to discuss such matters in the context of land claims, federal negotiators have consistently been denied the mandate to do so.
Canada Oil and Gas Act
This means that the government is misleading us and the northern peoples when it assures us that everything will be open to negotiation in the future. While such promises may be technically correct, past policies reveal the extent to which the government will actually negotiate. In the past it has refused to negotiate seriously on those matters which affect the economic rights of native peoples and on those matters which relate to their political rights. This represents the government's approach to land claims negotiations in the past and it represents the government's policy today. Yet, the minister would have us believe that everything will be negotiable later on, if only we will agree to their taking control of the resources now. I am unable to agree with this.
The present motion is a very interesting one although it is somewhat naive. It challenges the government on the very point I am addressing. If the government is sincere when it says that everything will remain negotiable for the purposes of land claims even after Bill C-48 is passed, then it should have no trouble supporting this particular motion. After all, it would only be an affirmation of the impression the government is earnestly trying to convey.
However, if the government is unwilling to support this motion, we will have no other choice but to question its future intentions. If it does not support the motion, we will have every reason to believe that its promises and assurances are hollow. Thus it will be a warning sign to all those who are looking toward land claims to provide a fair and equitable basis for participating in Canadian society-a warning that the government is not to be trusted.
It is my hope that the government will respond to this particular motion in a way as to allay any such conclusions. As I said, the motion is somewhat naive in that it was written by someone who had very good intentions and a good heart, but in the context of the current negotiations we could not agree with some parts of it. Generally I support the motion. Hopefully the government will do so, as it is the only motion which recognizes any justification for claims in relation to Bill C-48.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was listening very carefully to my colleague, the hon. member for Nunatsiaq (Mr. Ittinuar), especially since during the past year, as co-chairman of the Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on the Constitution, I was able to draw on his knowledge and experience of Canada's aboriginal peoples. His statements are always noted for their honesty and conviction, and the concerns he has expressed this afternoon cannot be dismissed lightly.
Monday evening I was listening while one of our hon. colleagues was asking a question-and I believe an answer is in order-in which he accused us, up to a point, of using Clause 34 of the constitutional resolution to confirm the rights of Canada's aboriginal peoples, and then turning around in Bill C-48 and ignoring completely any progressive measures we had taken previously in this respect.

October 21, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
I would like to read again Clause 34. I realize it represents the sum of concerted efforts by the hon. member for Nunat-siaq and several other members, especially my colleague, the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) and also, it must be said, of my colleague, the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp), all of whom emphasized the objectives Canada should pursue in this respect during the discussions we had on the subject last winter. Clause 34 of the constitutional resoluton provides, and I quote:
The aboriginal and treaty rights of the aboriginal peoples of Canada are hereby recognized and affirmed.
I feel this is extremely important. This is the basis for any action Parliament must take with respect to Canada's aboriginal peoples.
After listening to the comments made Monday evening, I happened to glance through the proceedings of the committee, and I was pleased to see that at least eight amendments had been made at the committee stage, probably thanks to representations by the hon. member for Nunatsiaq, the result being in most cases to confirm existing rights, in other words, to recognize the rights of Canada's aboriginal peoples. In fact, Mr. Speaker, and I would like to point this out, a clause was added to the bill. I am referring to Clause 5(2) and (3) which in fact specifically acknowledges that nothing in the bill changes any provisions previously agreed upon with Canada's aboriginal peoples. I have here Subclause (7) of the same clause, and I quote:
Nothing in this act abrogates or derogates from any aboriginal title, right or claim that pertained to the aboriginal peoples of Canada prior to the coming into force of this act.
This means that all matters which are being negotiated, all claims already pending and any rights that could be used as the basis for future claims are not affected by this bill. That is basically what is meant by Clause 5(7), an amendment that, I wish to emphasize, was made at the committee stage.
What will happen to subsequent claims? I believe that is a special concern of my colleague for Nunatsiaq. What will happen to claims that may be submitted once the bill has been passed or the constitutional resolution has been adopted? The hon. member mentioned that we wanted to withdraw from claims negotiations any lands that might contain oil or gas resources at the production stage. I wish to point out-he quite rightly mentioned claims that were settled through an agreement with COPE and he did so in great detail-that eight blocks of land have been accepted through COPE, seven blocks of 600 square miles each and one block of 800 square miles. It is true that within these blocks there are no claims with respect to gas or oil resources at the production stage. However, my colleague should know that the Dene and the Metis have, in this connection, submitted claims with respect to a well which is about to enter the production stage and is known as Norman Wells, a name that is so well known I shall not bother to translate it into French. Therefore, it is incorrect
to state that at this stage the government has refused to consider any possibility of negotiations that might concern wells or resources at the production stage or about to come into production.
When discussing the matter of claims to the lands in question, we must not forget the mechanism provided under Bill C-48 for future negotiations. Under the bill the governor in council may exclude from Crown lands any lands that may have been the subject of negotiations between the aboriginal peoples and the Canadian government. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) is given the power to exclude from Crown territorial lands any lands that may have been the object of a settlement between the aboriginal peoples and the Crown. Should wells be in operation in these lands compensation would be paid as in the case of any other resource recognized as being in production on such land. Nothing in the bill excludes from negotiations any wells that might be in production at the time of settlement. Moreover, the Constitutional resolution provides an extremely sound legal basis for negotiations and for compensation payments, in view of permits which may have been granted in the meantime or are granted once the bill is passed, until a fair system of compensation has been arrived at.
In my opinion, the amendments made at the committee stage-there are eight, I repeat-provide the mechanisms required to compensate each and every one of the native peoples of Canada who might have valid claims, judicially acknowledged by the courts, or again acknowledged in common agreement by the representatives of the federal Crown, and to ensure that the necessary financial or suitable compensations be the object of an agreement between the parties.
I believe that my colleague from Nunatsiaq rests his case on past experience to say, and rightfully so, that he has every reason to believe that they cannot rely on the good faith of the parties. He is right when he states that the best protection available to any minority is judicial protection, that is to say the protection of the rights enshrined in a law, whether it be that of the constitutional bill or Subclause 5(7) which may guarantee the fundamental rights of minority groups. In the context of native peoples in Canada, we can be glad that that will be the basis of all negotiations and all settlements with which we will have to come to grips in the near future.
In my opinion, that fundamentally changes the relationship which may have existed before between those peoples and the federal Crown. From the moment when the rights of the native peoples are directly enshrined in the constitutional statute, it can be seen that the federal negotiators will definitely not have the same room to manoeuvre. On the contrary, those peoples will have at their disposal the entire judicial arsenal to convince the authorities that the claims they may file are based on
October 21, 1981

aboriginal rights guaranteed as much by treaties, customs or conventions as by the wording of the act itself. And what is most fundamental, in my opinion, is that, and again I quote this part of Clause 34:
The aboriginal and treaty rights of the aboriginal peoples of Canada are hereby recognized and affirmed.
The rights confirmed by treaty are not the only ones to be mentioned. Mention is made of all the other rights stemming from customs, practices or else tacit acknowledgement. Therefore, nothing in this bill, especially under Subclause (7), restricts the claims which the aboriginal peoples of Canada have against the federal Crown with respect to those lands where, as of now, certain licences or certain permits may be issued. On the contrary, the bill gives to the minister responsible the discretion of forcing the companies and the business people that will henceforth develop those resources to take into account the cultural reality which is peculiar to those territories. The amendment related for instance to Subclause 10(2) and to Subclause 10(4) refers specifically to the participation of the aboriginal peoples, and I quote Subclause 10(2) (d), for it seems basic to me:
-equity participation by government and Canadians, including any aboriginal peoples of Canada who may be affected by the exploration agreement.
There was no mention in the previous legislation of the explicit participation of the aboriginal peoples of Canada in the equity of companies dealing with exploration of these resources. The bill now recognizes explicitly the absolute right of aboriginal peoples to equity in these companies. No provision of any previous legislation recognized this as explicitly. At the same time, Clause 10(4) deals with what are commonly known as affirmative action programs. Once again, nothing in any previous legislation provided for the possibility of including the aboriginal peoples for high technology and high responsibility employment. Once again, the minister responsible will be able to take action to ensure equitable participation, not only in equity, but also in the daily operation and management of these companies. It seems to me that enormous progress has been made.
Many groups have made representations to the minister, including the hon. member of the Christian hierarchy. As I pointed out earlier, these representations have resulted in specific amendments being made to the bill. I can assure the hon. member for Nunatsiaq that if I believed personally that this bill would jeopardize the explicit recognition of aboriginal rights to these lands and the resources they contain, if I had the least doubt that Subclause 7 of Clause 5 would reduce the rights of the native people to claim ownership of these resources, I would certainly not rise this afternoon to tell him that, as concerns what he and I are fighting for, that is to guarantee that the native peoples will from now on have an official share in Canadian resources. We are attempting today by a new initiative to reduce the possibility for them to have their claims settled by the courts since Clause 7 clearly shows
Canada Oil and Gas Act
that all our efforts since last fall are confirmed by this bill. It seems to me that the major progress accomplished in this bill is that from now on in any legislation which can affect the claims of aboriginal peoples, it will have to be recognized explicitly that no provision must affect or reduce in any way the rights of aboriginal peoples to claim their share of our resources. I repeat that Subclause 10(4) recognizes explicitly the full equity participation of aboriginal peoples.
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, we shall be faced with difficult situations in the years to come. When the parties involved negotiate settlements based on historically discriminatory situations and when we deal with peoples who have been able to develop their resources and put them to good use without jeopardizing them, it is quite obvious that there has to be some resentment and that we have to leave the past behind. However, I believe that the best way to meet this objective is to act on the basis of clear and explicit recognition of the rights of the aboriginal peoples, and I still believe that the best way to solve this problem is to pass as soon as possible the constitutional resolution, and especially Clause 34, which confirms the absolute right of the aboriginal people of Canada to everything that has been traditionally recognized by treaties and native rights.

In fact, a specific section has been put in so that not only will the federal government and native people define aboriginal claims or rights, but also the provinces. We all know that provinces are very protective of such things as land resources. This is one of the reasons many of the aboriginal or native peoples of this country question whether, in fact, they have any protection as far as land and resources are concerned, and also why they question whether such an amendment as this should be placed in the bill in order to affirm that, in fact, they have some claim to land and resources in the north under this bill.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio)
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the question put by the hon. member, because it is ultimately at the root of the

October 21, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
issue of native rights. It is fair to suggest that when we attempt to define native rights, we are faced with a major difficulty. This is why the wording of Section 34 is so vague. It is both vague and all encompassing.
Had we included in Clause 34 an enumeration of either a restrictive or indicative nature of the kind of rights that could be included or the kind of things those rights might have contained, we would have been faced with insuperable difficulties. Clearly, the provinces, as he rightly suggests, are most reluctant to enter into a discussion process where the contents of those rights would be specified. The hon. member for Provencher, who took part along with us in all those discussions, was the first to suggest that. Within the framework of the constitutional conference envisaged in Section 36, the hon. member realized this, and I quote Section 36(2):
-respecting constitutional matters that directly affect the aboriginal peoples of Canada, including the identification and definition of the rights of those peoples to be included in the Constitution of Canada.
Committee members unanimously recognized that had we gone into that process at this stage, we would never have seen the end of it, for the very good reason that those rights change. They take greater dimensions along the years. Current native land claims at this time are much more extensive than ten or 20 years ago. And it is better to have an over-all protection in principle stating the rights as a whole rather than to try, by way of an enumeration, even if it is indicative, to restrict the object of those rights. However, if I may answer more directly the question, native rights include both rights to the land and rights to the resources. When earlier settlements were reached with the COPE group, the hon. member for Nunatsiaq rightly suggested that the matter of resources already being explored were excluded.
But matters have changed since. I even mentioned to him that concerning the claims of the Dene and Metis, we were ready to consider, within the framework of over-all negotiations, the assessment and inclusion of resources already or close to being developed. Therefore, there is nothing in the matter of native claims that precludes claims on these lands or resources, whether surface or subsurface. The matter in my view must be examined in the over-all context of Section 34. In other words, what is involved here is the over-all rights, and those rights include social rights, property rights and other rights connected with the occupancy of the land.

Mr. Speaker, although he is also quite young the hon. member knows how to be cutting. It is true that at the committee stage we altered Section 34 which had a rather negative approach to take a more affirmative approach, which is to say, there are some absolute rights and they must be respected and enforced. However, there is a basic difference between the constitutional resolution and an act of Parliament. And the hon. member knows quite well that when we want to exempt a previous statute from the application of legislation, the negative approach is taken.
In spite of all previous comments, this bill suggests, and the hon. member who is a lawyer is well aware of that exclusive clause, that Clause 57 does not exclude but recognizes the full application of the Constitution Act since it states that this legislation does not interfere with the titles, rights or claims of the native people of Canada, which they held before the coming into force of the legislation.
Consequently, what is stated under Clause 34 as being the absolute right of native people is not at all excluded from or denied in paragraph (7). Clause 7 says that if you thought that Bill C-48 encroached on the rights of the native people as recognized in previous legislation, that is Clause 34 of the Constitution Act, you are mistaken, because that legislation is fully enforced. This is the thrust of Clause 7 but in simple and everyday terms. Therefore, what the hon. member suggests is that Clause 7 of that legislation should recognize the full application of Clause 34 of the Constitution Act. It is in short

what he would suggest as an amendment or as an assertion of natives' rights. But the hon. member is aware also that at this stage, at least the debate on this aspect of Section 34 has been delayed and that there is no way we could refer directly to Section 34. speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio)
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad the hon. member for Nunatsiaq asked this question which, in fact, is in two parts. The first one concerns naturally the equity issue: What reasonable, acceptable and responsible share in the ownership of these resources should the aboriginal people hold? And the second one, which is a corollary: How are we going to determine what is fair and what is not? That is essentially the object of his question.
I indicated a while ago that, once Clause 34 of the constitutional act has been adopted, we will have to start new negotia-
Canada Oil and Gas Act
tions based on the new legislation. Therefore, all the claims which the aboriginal people may have on federal Crown lands will have to be based essentially on ancestral rights or treaties, and no longer on wide discussions concerning their legal basis. When the time comes to determine what is fair, we will have to decide within the global context of the claims which every group will want to bring to the negotiation table, what the Inuit propose, what the Dene and the Metis propose, what obviously COPE has already started to negotiate and what the CYI has proposed or intends to propose for debate. The share of equity to be attributed to each of the aboriginal peoples, with regard to the lands concerned will be based essentially on the rights recognized in Clause 34. If the conclusion is reached, through arbitration or judicial process, that their share of equity is to exceed that of the majority, the matter will be settled essentially through arbitration or judicial process. There will no longer be any paternalistic stand to be taken saying: the symbolic participation of our aboriginals must be saved, they must have some equity. The claims of the native people then will be based exclusively on their rights. Why? Because for the first time those rights will be recognized in our statutes. Therein will lie the difference in future negotiations. I can tell my hon. colleague that the negotiations in which we took part in the past easily took on a paternalistic hue, but will no longer do so because the rights of Canadians will be enshrined as those of an adult people full master of its destiny and fully able to determine through arbitration, judicial process or free negotiation what the respective share of each will be in the equity and development of those resources. That, to my mind, is the essential difference; this should reassure the hon. member with regard to the meaning of the word "equity" or "participation" will be given in the administration, the management of those resources.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the minister might entertain one more short question. I think he has given us some fairly good insight into a problem we have been raising for some time. The dilemma we have been expressing over a period of time relates to the permission for oil and gas development to proceed under this legislation in which no specifics are written. This is largely a discretionary piece of legislation, with the power to make decisions affecting aboriginal people left in the hands of the minister. As my colleague, the hon. member for Nunatsiaq (Mr. Ittinuar), has said, the clause providing equity is not really worth very much. What we have to do is to expand and define some of these things.
We suspect that the oil and gas development in my area will proceed very rapidly. Some of the aboriginal people in those communities have not even reached the state of defining their claims. There is a group of them in Ottawa right now who have defined their claim and would like to have some response before the oil and gas development proceeds. Some claims have been made and others have not even been defined at this time, yet the oil and gas developments are proceeding.

October 21, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
Once this development proceeds, it will shape the communities. The infrastructure will already be in place and the patterns of production and exploration will be completed. What we have been trying to do is to get more definition in order to allow the pacing of development so the people in the region can participate meaningfully in the planning of activities and in the activities themselves. If this legislation goes ahead at the rate it is now proceeding, these people will be left out, and their land claims will not be recognized and they will have no benefit. I would like to hear some comment in that regard.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for affording me the opportunity to answer these questions because, as the hon. member mentioned, these are problems we will have to address in any future legislation dealing with or affecting the rights of native peoples, and I do not think it useless for my colleagues to become aware of the situation as are those hon. members who raised these issues.
The problem which my hon. colleague brings up is a very real one. What will happen with future claims which we cannot provide for just now or what happens with present claims which some native groups or peoples cannot make at this time. This is a very important issue since their rights are affected with regard to resource ownership and management as well as their very lives and environment as the hon. member mentioned. What must be recognized at this stage is that Clause 34 acknowledges and affirms their rights, and if it is shown in the settlement of claims over these lands that these people had strict ownership rights with regard to these resources, they are entitled to a generous compensation either of a financial nature, of which there are many examples, or through lands that could be made available to them in similar conditions. We cannot, at this point, provide for everything and some groups may indeed be in dire circumstances, but the important thing is that their rights are protected. They are protected because the ownership rights of these people over these resources are recognized.
When we say in Clause 34 that aboriginal rights are hereby confirmed, the basic right remains, regardless of whether these rights are confirmed now or will be in the future. There will be some form of compensation and it will be possible in the settlement of the claim to offer these people the same protection and access to the resources they would have had if they had made their claim in due time. Yet the hon. member must admit that it is impossible to provide for everything. Many of the native peoples who appeared before the committee could not define aboriginal rights. It is an evolutionary notion. Its contents increase rather than decrease. Its meaning and its implications increase in keeping with our knowledge of history, treaties and past practices. Therefore the implications of this recognition or rights will not lessen, they will extend, and will only place more responsibility on representatives of the Crown
and on all corporations which may become involved in those areas. That is why I want to reassure the hon. member that this aspect and these implications are protected because the rights of those people will be upheld, and all claims that may be laid will be based on full and total ownership of these lands and resources.
